intro: Donald Betts opens Kinderszenen with a G-major tune that seems to remember its own childhood. Between the melody and the bass, little triplets keep turning.

sections.label: A · A tune over triplets
sections.mNote: Eight bars in G major, repeated

sections.label: B · Paired notes, then a pause
A′ · The G-major tune returns
sections.mNote: The melody begins on D this time

sections.label: B · Paired notes once more
sections.mNote: The second strain repeats, including the returning tune

cues.title: A tune over triplets
cues.text: The melody leaps from B to G and comes down F♯–E–D. Under it, triplets pass between the hands while the bass keeps its own two-beat tread. Three things happen at once, softly.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 3, bars 1–8. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The tune comes round
cues.text: The same eight bars begin again. The high G is still the melody’s favourite note; beneath it, B♭ briefly colours the accompaniment before the music settles back into G major.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 3: repeat after bar 8; B♭ in the triplet accompaniment of bars 1 and 3.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A page for Marie
cues.text: In 1847 Schumann gives the manuscript of this piece to his sister-in-law Marie Wieck. It is now in the Robert-Schumann-Haus in Zwickau: the only complete autograph of any of the thirteen Kinderszenen.
cues.evidence: Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (Robert-Schumann-Haus Zwickau, 2013), item 5, autograph 3702–A1. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: The melody grows a second voice
transitions.to: B · Paired notes, then a pause
transitions.how: The G-major ending opens into E minor. The right hand now sings in pairs of notes, beginning with G and B, while the triplets continue underneath. Schumann keeps the two-beat pulse and marks the new phrase piano.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 3, bars 8–10; E–B–E accompaniment under G and B at bar 9.

transitions.title: A pause before G major
transitions.from: B · Paired notes, then a pause
transitions.how: A ritardando and fermata hold back the end of the new phrase. The triplets then resume beneath the G-major tune, marked piano. Its first note is D; the leap to G and the descending answer are familiar.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 3, bars 13–16; melody checked against Ying-Chun Liu’s Mutopia transcription, based on Leichte Stücke (1900).

transitions.title: Back to the paired notes
transitions.how: The G-major cadence reaches a long B in the melody. The repeat sends the pianist straight back to the paired G and B over E-minor accompaniment. The six-bar excursion, the fermata and the homecoming all happen again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 3, repeat from bar 22 to bar 9.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The sources do not say which printed edition Donald Betts played from. Schumann’s Kinderszenen exist in a pre-publication printing, the 1839 first edition and its revised second issue, and Clara Schumann’s later edition; the recording is not matched to any of them here.

composer.epithet: A bookseller’s son who put lovers, masks and arguments into piano music, and made criticism a form of friendship.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The books offered twins, disguises, conversations that wandered away from their subject and returned by an unexpected door. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The music changes partners every few bars.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828, moved to Heidelberg the following year, and finally persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil who had much to catch up on. By 1832, paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and began building a life at the writing desk.
